name: Kyoto
description: Central Kyoto, from Kyoto Station and its tower to the Imperial Palace gardens: temples among low tiled roofs, the Kamo River's banks, and streets laid out for an emperor in 794.

bridges.note: The Kamo River's bridges, over the riverbed the aerial photograph shows; forms from Kyoto City (京の橋しるべ) and each bridge's record.

三条大橋.note: 1950, steel girders under the hinoki railing and its bronze giboshi

四条大橋.note: 1942, a continuous girder, the 1965 white railing

七条大橋.note: 1913, five concrete arches of about 15 m

加茂大橋.note: 1931, steel Gerber girders under a stone balustrade

water.note: No sea: Kyoto is 25-80 m above it. Its rivers, canals and ponds are drawn at their own level (inland, pipeline/inland_water.py); the Nijo Castle moats are the landmark's own.

inland.note: The Kamo River in its bed at the 5 m laser survey's level; the Takase River, Shirakawa and the Misosogi between stone walls (about 1-2 m down to a shallow flow, read from photographs); the Kamo Canal and the Biwako Canal at Okazaki between stone walls about 2.5 and 1.8 m down. The Horikawa from Oshikoji up to the map's edge is a sunken promenade (Kyoto City's water restoration, 1997-2008): a paved floor between its stone walls about 2.6 m under the street, the stream down its middle, and steps down from the crossings (where OpenStreetMap maps them); its features where Kyoto City's summary of the works places them in its zones A-E, lettered from the south (#322): seating steps between Nijo and Oshikoji (A); the stream along the west wall and stepped drops, the floor stepping down with them, between Marutamachi and Takeyamachi (B); a lawn and a slab over the stream between Shimochojamachi and Demizu (C); the stream winding under two slabs, and below Modoribashi the audience's steps on the west wall and the floor as a stage with the stream along the east wall (D); stepping stones by Horikawa Daiichi-bashi (Commons photographs). The depth, the widths, the tiers and the drops' spacing are read from photographs, not measured; 9.9 m between the walls from a maintenance tender's bed area (9.85 m on average).

susuki.note: Susuki (trees.json susuki, #326): the silver grass of the Kamo's banks and sandbars, over the rank vegetation OpenStreetMap maps along the river (natural=scrub and grassland within 12 m of its water: susuki, ogi and reeds, unmown between the paths and the water), and any mapped meadow (Overture base land, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; pipeline/grasses.py). Its heads stand from mid August to spring (web/trees.js).

trees.note: Species are not mapped; the mix is a guess from the cities' street-tree surveys and the parks' own guides: ginkgo and zelkova (keyaki) are Japan's commonest street trees, with plane trees and camphor; the woods are the laurel forest's evergreen broadleaves and camphors, with zelkovas, black pines, maples and a few cedars (sugi, standing for hinoki too). Areas give the parks and precincts known for their own trees a mix of their own; their outlines are OpenStreetMap's (pipeline/tree_areas.py). Somei-yoshino cherries (sakura) line Tokyo's streets after the ginkgo and the zelkova, and stand in the parks' lawns and along the rivers and moats; areas give the places known for them a mix of their own.

areas.name: Takase River
areas.note: Kiyamachi-dori's cherries over the Takase canal (an elm stands in for the willows among them).

areas.name: Shirakawa
areas.note: Gion Shirakawa: Somei-yoshino and weeping cherries and weeping willows (elms stand in) over the stream by Tatsumi Bridge.

areas.name: Kyoto Gyoen
areas.note: The Gyoen's black pines stand on its lawns and along its gravel avenues; its groves are broadleaf (mukunoki, enoki, zelkova, camphor) and maples. Its cherries: the Konoe-tei's weeping cherries (itozakura), and double cherries in mid April.

areas.name: Nijo Castle
areas.note: Nijo Castle's cherry garden and Seiryu-en: some fifty varieties, from the weeping cherries to the late double ones.

areas.name: Nishi Honganji
areas.note: The 'upside-down ginkgo' (sakasa-icho) and the precinct's ginkgos.

walls.note: Earthen precinct walls (tsuiji-bei) on a stone plinth under a tiled coping, in yellow-ochre plaster (pipeline/walls.py). OpenStreetMap maps the walls of the Gosho and the Sento Gosho as buildings without a height; 4.5 m to the ridge is read from photographs against people at the gates, not measured. Sanjusangen-do's Taiko-bei keeps its PLATEAU height (5.0 m; 5.3 m published).

lines.name: Kyoto Gosho and Sento Gosho: suji-bei with five white lines, the highest rank

protection.title: No statutory sun rule for public places
protection.summary: Kyoto protects its skyline with height limits (a cap of 31 m in the busiest districts) and Japan limits shadows on homes with the Building Standards Act, but neither protects sun on parks. Sun on these places is measured for information, not tested against a rule.
protection.source_note: No legal window is transcribed for these places, so each is shown for 10:00-14:00 and none is marked protected.
protection.reading_note: Heights come from Project PLATEAU, measured from aerial survey in 2020-2021, so buildings finished since are missing or low.
protection.tip: Tip: try a plot just south of the Imperial Gardens in winter.

tour.title: The capital of a thousand years
tour.text: Emperor Kanmu laid out Heian-kyo here in 794, a grid copied from China's capital, and the city still lives on it. Children learn its streets from a song: Maru, Take, Ebisu, Ni, Oshi, Oike...

tour.title: Kyoto Tower
tour.text: A white-and-red candle of 131 m, lit for the city in 1964 and meant to look like a lighthouse over a sea of tiled roofs. Its deck at 100 m sees the whole basin to the hills.

tour.title: Higashi Honganji
tour.text: The Founder's Hall is one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. When it was rebuilt, women gave their hair to braid the ropes that hauled its beams; one rope is still on show.

tour.title: A city that stays low
tour.text: Kyoto keeps its skyline down by law, so temple roofs still rise over the houses and the hills stay in view from every street. Only the tower and the station stand out.

tour.title: Winter on the roofs
tour.text: The winter sun stays low over Kyoto, and long shadows fall across the tiled roofs all day. It's the season for hot tofu at Nanzen-ji and a quiet temple garden.

tour.title: The Imperial Palace gardens
tour.text: Kyoto Gyoen, the palace's great park of gravel avenues, plum and cherry groves. On a winter noon {sun:京都御苑|12-21|12:00}% of it is in the sun, a good place for a bench and a can of hot coffee.

tour.title: The Kamo River at dusk
tour.text: When the sun drops behind the western hills, Kyoto comes down to the river. Couples sit evenly spaced along the bank, and in summer the restaurants of Pontocho open their wooden terraces over the water.

hero.note: Kyoto Station's north forecourt, Shiokoji-dori and Kyoto Tower Building's faces, modelled finely (cities/kyoto/hero.py, blender/build_hero.py, docs/HERO.md)

npcs.name: Haruka
idle: Kyoto Tower opened in 1964, the same year as the Shinkansen. People hated it then. Now it's how you know you're home.

npcs.name: Brother Sozen
idle: The wooden hall behind me is among the largest in the world. Please do not run in the temple grounds.

npcs.name: Mr. Tanaka
idle: I came down from Tokyo on the Nozomi this morning, about two hours and a quarter. Meetings all day, then the last train back.
Tokyo has towers everywhere. Here the roofs stay low, and I think I like it more.

npcs.name: Mrs. Nakamura
idle: Tsukemono, fresh today! The market has fed Kyoto for about four hundred years.
Kyoto houses are narrow at the street and very deep behind. We call them eel's beds.

npcs.name: Ken
idle: Tokugawa Ieyasu built Nijo Castle in 1603. Walk the corridors of the Ninomaru Palace and the floorboards sing like nightingales, to warn of intruders.

npcs.name: Yui
npcs.role: Student on a school trip from Tokyo
idle: Shugaku ryoko! Everyone in Japan comes to Kyoto in their school uniform, once. We have a bus at four, so I need to be quick.
My class is from Setagaya. Tokyo is so tall, and I did not expect Kyoto to feel so flat.

lines.on_open: Every walk done. Report back to Haruka at Kyoto Station, under the tower.

quests.title: Welcome to Kyoto Station
talk: Konnichiwa, welcome to Kyoto. I'm Haruka; I grew up two streets from the station. That's Kyoto Tower behind me: 131 m, and nothing else in the city comes close.

Three walks, in any order. The temple and the low city: Brother Sozen, at Higashi Honganji just north of here. The market: Mrs. Nakamura, in Nishiki. The castle: Ken, at Nijo, and then a schoolgirl with a question about the winter sun.

The helicopter is on the station plaza and taxis wait right here: a hand up at the kerb (Y). WASD or the arrow keys to walk, Shift to run, drag to look around, E to talk. Where will you start? いってらっしゃい.

choices.text: The temple and the low city: Brother Sozen, at Higashi Honganji
The market: Mrs. Nakamura, in Nishiki
The castle: Ken, at Nijo Castle

quests.title: The wooden hall
talk: Welcome. This is the Founder's Hall, the Goei-do. It was rebuilt in 1895 and is among the largest wooden buildings in the world.
Look at the roofs around it. Kyoto has always been low. Mr. Tanaka is in the office streets near Karasuma and Shijo, a long walk north. He can tell you why.

steps.text: Walk north to Mr. Tanaka at Karasuma-Shijo

quests.title: A city that stays low
talk: Ah, a visitor! I am in from Tokyo too. Look around: very few buildings here pass 31 m, and the rules want it that way.
In 2007 the city lowered its height limits, 31 m at most even here in the centre, and banned signs on the rooftops. Even the convenience stores dress in quieter colours.
Go and eat something at Nishiki Market, a few blocks east. Mrs. Nakamura will feed you.

steps.text: Find Mrs. Nakamura in Nishiki Market

quests.title: Eel's beds
talk: Ah, a hungry one! Try a pickle. Look how narrow the shops are: three or four metres wide, and very deep. That is how Kyoto was taxed, by the width of your front.
We shut at about six. Come back after dark, when the shutters are down: they have Jakuchu's paintings on them, cockerels and vegetables. He was a greengrocer's son from this very street.

steps.text: Walk Nishiki Market after dark, when the shutters are down

quests.title: Nightingale floors
talk: Welcome to Nijo Castle. Ieyasu had it built in 1603 as the Tokugawa shogun's Kyoto residence.
From here, go to the Imperial Gardens: Yui is there on her school trip. She wanted to know whether the sun reaches the gravel in winter.

steps.text: Find Yui in the Kyoto Imperial Gardens

quests.title: A place in the sun
talk: Konnichiwa! Is it true the sun stays so low in winter? Tokyo feels dark between the buildings.
On 21 December at noon, {sun:京都御苑|12-21|12:00}% of the Kyoto Gyoen gets direct sun. On 21 June it is {sun:京都御苑|6-21|12:00}%. No rule protects it.
Find a sunny spot in the gardens at noon on 21 December. The sun meter under the map tells you when you're in it.

steps.text: Stand in direct sun in the Kyoto Imperial Gardens, 12:00 to 14:00 on 21 December

quests.title: From the station to the Palace
talk: おかえりやす, welcome back. A wooden hall, a pickle, a castle and a patch of winter sun on the Palace gravel: that's Kyoto, from the station to the Palace.
Take the helicopter from the station plaza if you want to see how flat it really is: the streets still keep the grid of 794.
The city is yours. Change the time of day, or fly anywhere.

game.blurb: Walk Kyoto under the real sun. Talk to the people who know it, from the monks of Higashi Honganji to a salaryman up from Tokyo, and fly over the grid Kyoto was laid out on in 794.
